topic: Day 2 · Acute-on-Chronic Complications in the Diabetic Patient
speakerTitle: Consultant in Acute Medicine with a special interest in the Diabetic Foot
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit & Multidisciplinary Foot Service
speakerBio: Acute physician embedded in the multidisciplinary diabetic foot team who has watched too many limbs lost to the phrase 'it doesn't hurt' and too many infarcts missed because 'he didn't look cardiac'.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 64-year-old man with a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department feeling "washed out and a bit breathless" since the morning. No chest pain. Observations are unremarkable; the triage note reads "?viral, ?anxiety." His ECG is not done for three hours because "he doesn't look like a cardiac patient." When it is finally recorded it shows an evolving anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, hours old. Diabetes did two things to this man: it furred his coronaries, and — through autonomic neuropathy — it switched off the pain that would have brought him in on time. Today is about the acute emergencies that hide behind diabetes, and the low threshold you need to catch them.

1 · 🕵️ The governing idea — diabetes masks and accelerates

Chronic diabetes changes the presentation of acute illness in two dangerous directions at once:

  • It masks — autonomic neuropathy blunts the warning symptoms (chest pain, the adrenergic response to hypoglycaemia), so emergencies present late and atypically.
  • It accelerates — hyperglycaemia, microvascular disease and immune dysfunction let infections explode into limb- and life-threatening territory far faster than in non-diabetics.
In the diabetic patient, absence of the classic symptom is not reassurance — it is the disease hiding the diagnosis. Lower every threshold: for ACS work-up, for imaging the hot foot, for suspecting a necrotising infection.

2 · 🦶 The diabetic foot emergency

A red, hot, swollen diabetic foot is a time-critical emergency, not a clinic problem. Neuropathy removes protective pain, peripheral arterial disease starves the tissue, and hyperglycaemia cripples neutrophils — so a trivial ulcer can become deep sepsis, wet gangrene or a necrotising infection within a day or two. The two questions to answer fast:

Is it infection or Charcot?

FeatureInfection / deep sepsisAcute Charcot neuroarthropathy
SkinUlcer, discharge, spreading erythema, trackingIntact skin (often), diffuse warmth & swelling
Systemic upsetFever, raised WCC/CRP, rising glucose, sepsisUsually systemically well
Response to elevationErythema persistsRedness often reduces on elevation (vascular, not septic)
DeformityMay have underlying osteomyelitis / collectionProgressive bony collapse → "rocker-bottom" foot
Immediate riskLimb / life — sepsis, spreading necrosisJoint destruction if weight-borne — needs offloading/immobilisation
⚠️ Classify the threat immediately

Every acute diabetic foot is triaged as limb-threatening or life-threatening: spreading cellulitis, deep collection, wet gangrene, crepitus/gas, or systemic sepsis mandate same-day surgical review, urgent imaging (X-ray then MRI for deep infection/osteomyelitis), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and often urgent surgical debridement or drainage. Do not "trial oral antibiotics and review in clinic." Assess the vascular supply (a limb that is also ischaemic needs revascularisation) and always probe-to-bone (a positive probe-to-bone strongly suggests osteomyelitis).

💡 The one-liner

"The red hot swollen diabetic foot is limb-threatening until an X-ray, a surgeon and a vascular opinion say otherwise." A missed foot infection is measured in amputations.

3 · 🫀 Silent MI and atypical ACS

Autonomic neuropathy blunts or abolishes anginal pain. Diabetics — especially long-standing, elderly, and those with established neuropathy — present with acute coronary syndromes as breathlessness, fatigue, nausea, sweating, confusion, collapse, or unexplained hyperglycaemia/DKA rather than crushing chest pain. "Silent" MI is common and carries a worse prognosis, partly because it presents late.

  • Have a very low threshold for ACS work-up in any unwell diabetic — ECG and troponin for vague breathlessness, malaise, nausea, new arrhythmia, unexplained hyperglycaemia or "off legs."
  • Do the ECG early — do not let "doesn't look cardiac" delay it.
  • New or worsening hyperglycaemia can be the presenting sign of an infarct (stress response) — treat the sugar AND look for the cause.

4 · 📈 Acute hyperglycaemia worsens acute illness — stroke and ACS

Acute hyperglycaemia (whether known diabetes or stress hyperglycaemia in a previously non-diabetic) is not just a marker of severity — it independently worsens outcomes in acute stroke and myocardial infarction through impaired collateral flow, oxidative stress, thrombogenicity and larger infarct size.

  • In acute stroke and ACS, hyperglycaemia is associated with larger infarcts and worse outcomes; the aim is to avoid both marked hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia.
  • Target moderate control, not tight control — landmark critical-care data (NICE-SUGAR) showed that intensive tight glycaemic control caused more hypoglycaemia and higher mortality; a moderate target (commonly ~6–10, up to ~12 mmol/L) is safer for acutely ill inpatients.
  • Manage with insulin (often a variable-rate infusion in the acute phase), not with a return to oral agents.
💡 The Goldilocks rule

In the acutely ill diabetic, glucose control is a "not too high, not too low" problem. Hyperglycaemia enlarges infarcts; iatrogenic hypoglycaemia kills. Aim for the moderate middle and check glucose often.

5 · 🔄 Diabetic autonomic complications that ambush the acute team

Autonomic neuropathy touches every organ that a nerve controls, and each variant can masquerade as, or complicate, an acute presentation:

SystemAutonomic problemAcute pitfall
CardiacBlunted pain, resting tachycardia, silent ischaemiaSilent MI; poor tolerance of arrhythmia; sudden death risk
GIGastroparesis — delayed gastric emptyingVomiting, erratic glucose, aspiration risk at anaesthesia; mimics obstruction
VascularPostural hypotensionFalls, collapse, "?sepsis" hypotension; poor response to standing
BladderNeurogenic bladder / retentionSilent large-volume retention, recurrent UTI/urosepsis, post-op retention
Hypo awarenessLoss of adrenergic warning symptomsHypoglycaemia unawareness → severe hypos with no warning

6 · 🔥 Rapidly progressive infections in poorly controlled diabetes

Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and, in ketoacidosis, provides the acidic iron-rich milieu certain organisms love. Diabetics own a rogues' gallery of fulminant infections that non-diabetics rarely see — recognise them because hours matter:

InfectionClueAction
Necrotising fasciitisPain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, crepitus, skin dusky/bullous, systemic toxicityImmediate surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics + resuscitation; imaging must NOT delay theatre
Rhino-cerebral mucormycosisPoorly controlled/DKA patient with facial/orbital pain, black nasal/palatal eschar, proptosis, cranial nerve signsUrgent ENT/surgical debridement + liposomal amphotericin B; correct the acidosis/hyperglycaemia
Emphysematous pyelonephritisSevere pyelonephritis not improving; gas in the renal parenchyma on CTResuscitation, IV antibiotics, urgent urology — drainage or nephrectomy
Emphysematous cholecystitisCholecystitis with gas in the gallbladder wall/lumen on imaging; gangrene/perforation riskIV antibiotics + urgent surgery/cholecystectomy or drainage
Malignant otitis externaElderly diabetic, severe ear pain, granulation in the canal (Pseudomonas)Prolonged anti-pseudomonal therapy; risk of skull-base osteomyelitis
⚠️ Gas and pain-out-of-proportion are red flags

In a diabetic, gas in soft tissue or an organ, or pain wildly out of proportion to visible findings, means a necrotising or emphysematous infection until proven otherwise. These are surgical emergencies — the antibiotics buy time, but the knife is the treatment. Do not wait for the erythema to "declare itself."

7 · 📋 Complication → clue → action

Hidden emergencyThe clue that betrays itImmediate action
Silent MI / atypical ACSBreathless, nausea, collapse, unexplained hyperglycaemia — no chest painEarly ECG + troponin; treat as ACS
Diabetic foot sepsisRed hot swollen foot, ulcer, systemic upsetSame-day surgery + imaging + IV antibiotics; classify limb/life threat
Charcot footWarm swollen foot, systemically well, redness settles on elevationOffload/immobilise, imaging, specialist referral
Necrotising fasciitisPain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin, toxicityStraight to theatre + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
MucormycosisDKA/uncontrolled + black nasal/palatal eschar, orbital signsUrgent debridement + liposomal amphotericin B
Emphysematous pyelo/cholecystitisSevere infection + gas on imagingResuscitate + IV antibiotics + urgent surgical/urological source control
GastroparesisRecurrent vomiting, erratic glucose, aspirationProkinetics, aspiration precautions, glucose control
Postural hypotensionFalls, collapse, lying/standing BP dropFluids, medication review, treat cause
Neurogenic bladderRecurrent UTI, silent retentionBladder scan, catheterise, treat urosepsis
☠️ M&M — the foot that cost a leg

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and known neuropathy attended the emergency department with a "grumbling" ulcer under the first metatarsal head and a warm, mildly swollen forefoot. He had no pain (the neuropathy saw to that) and only a low-grade temperature. He was given a week of oral flucloxacillin and a foot-clinic appointment for eleven days later. Because it didn't hurt, he kept walking on it. Four days on he became septic; by the time he re-presented he had a deep plantar-space abscess, spreading necrosis and osteomyelitis of the metatarsals, with an ischaemic component nobody had assessed. He needed an emergency below-knee amputation. Root causes: a limb-threatening foot managed as an outpatient cellulitis; no urgent X-ray, no probe-to-bone, no vascular assessment, no same-day surgical review; and the neuropathic absence of pain misread as reassurance rather than the danger sign it was. The teaching: the red hot swollen diabetic foot is an emergency, and 'it doesn't hurt' makes it more dangerous, not less.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Diabetes masks and accelerates. Absent symptoms are the disease hiding — lower every threshold.
  2. The red hot swollen foot is a limb- and life-threatening emergency — same-day surgery, imaging, IV antibiotics, vascular assessment; distinguish infection from Charcot but treat sepsis first.
  3. Silent/atypical MI is common — do an early ECG and troponin for breathlessness, collapse, nausea or unexplained hyperglycaemia in any diabetic.
  4. Acute hyperglycaemia worsens stroke and ACS outcomes, but tight control kills (NICE-SUGAR) — aim for the moderate middle (~6–10 mmol/L).
  5. Autonomic neuropathy ambushes you — gastroparesis, postural hypotension, neurogenic bladder, hypo unawareness.
  6. Diabetics get fulminant infections — necrotising fasciitis, mucormycosis, emphysematous pyelonephritis/cholecystitis; gas and pain-out-of-proportion mean the knife, not just antibiotics.

moderatorQs.q: A long-standing diabetic presents with vague breathlessness, nausea and no chest pain. Why does diabetes make you more, not less, worried about ACS here?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because in diabetes autonomic neuropathy blunts or abolishes anginal pain, so a myocardial infarction presents 'silently' or atypically — as breathlessness, fatigue, nausea, sweating, collapse, a new arrhythmia, or unexplained hyperglycaemia/DKA — rather than as crushing chest pain. These silent infarcts present later and carry a worse prognosis. So the absence of chest pain is not reassurance; it is exactly what the disease does. I would have a very low threshold: an early 12-lead ECG and troponin for any unwell diabetic with these vague features, and I would not let 'he doesn't look cardiac' delay the ECG.

moderatorQs.q: How do you distinguish an acutely infected diabetic foot from acute Charcot neuroarthropathy at the bedside, and does it change your immediate management?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both give a warm, swollen foot, but the discriminators are: infection usually has a portal (ulcer/discharge), spreading erythema, systemic upset (fever, raised WCC/CRP, rising glucose), whereas acute Charcot classically occurs in a systemically well patient, often with intact skin, and the redness tends to reduce on elevating the leg (it is vascular, not septic), progressing to bony collapse and a rocker-bottom deformity. It absolutely changes management: infection/sepsis is treated first and fast — same-day surgical review, imaging, IV antibiotics, vascular assessment, because it is limb- and life-threatening — while Charcot needs urgent offloading/immobilisation and specialist referral to prevent joint destruction. When in doubt, treat the limb as infected until sepsis is excluded.

moderatorQs.q: In an acutely ill diabetic with a high glucose after a stroke or MI, why not just drive the sugar down tightly to normal?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because tight glycaemic control harms acutely ill patients. The NICE-SUGAR trial showed that intensive control aiming for near-normal glucose caused far more hypoglycaemia and higher mortality than a moderate target. Acute hyperglycaemia does independently worsen stroke and MI outcomes (larger infarcts, worse collateral flow, thrombogenicity), so you do want to bring it down — but into a moderate range (commonly ~6–10, up to ~12 mmol/L), not to normal, because iatrogenic hypoglycaemia is itself dangerous in an ischaemic brain and heart. It is a 'not too high, not too low' problem, best managed with insulin (often a variable-rate infusion acutely) and frequent monitoring.

audienceQs.q: A poorly-controlled diabetic in DKA has facial pain and a blackish area on the hard palate. What am I worried about and how fast do I move?
audienceQs.answerHTML: You are worried about rhino-cerebral mucormycosis — an angioinvasive fungal infection that thrives in the acidotic, hyperglycaemic, iron-rich milieu of poorly-controlled diabetes and DKA. The black necrotic eschar on the palate or nasal mucosa, with facial/orbital pain, proptosis or cranial nerve signs, is the classic picture, and it spreads toward the orbit and brain within hours to days. Move immediately: urgent ENT/maxillofacial surgical review for debridement, start liposomal amphotericin B, take urgent imaging and tissue for fungal microscopy/culture, and aggressively correct the acidosis and hyperglycaemia. Delay costs the eye, then the life.

audienceQs.q: My diabetic patient has severe leg pain that seems way worse than the mild redness I can see, and I think I can feel crackling under the skin. Antibiotics and review in the morning?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — that is a surgical emergency tonight. Pain out of proportion to the visible signs plus crepitus (crackling gas under the skin) in a diabetic is necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise, and it kills fast. Do not wait for the redness to 'declare itself' and do not let imaging delay theatre. Escalate immediately for urgent surgical debridement, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and anaerobes, per local policy), resuscitate, and get senior surgical and critical-care input now. Antibiotics buy time, but the definitive treatment is surgical excision of the necrotic tissue.

audienceQs.q: One of our long-standing diabetics keeps 'going off' and getting confused, and his sugars swing wildly, but he never complains of feeling low. Why?
audienceQs.answerHTML: He likely has hypoglycaemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy: the adrenergic warning symptoms (sweating, tremor, palpitations) that normally alert someone to a falling glucose are blunted or absent, so he goes straight to the neuroglycopenic stage — confusion, odd behaviour, 'going off' — without warning. Combined with possible gastroparesis causing erratic absorption, his glucose can swing widely. Practically: check a capillary glucose every time he 'goes off' rather than waiting for him to report symptoms, review whether his insulin/sulfonylurea is too aggressive, aim for slightly more relaxed targets to rebuild awareness, and flag him to the diabetes team.
